clue.text: Ever so rude, Oxford's top man when solving

definitions.text: Ever so rude, Oxford's top man when solving

indicators.note: solving a puzzle means working its pieces out, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, here of Oxford's

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A grumpy Oxford detective is famously short-tempered while cracking a case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when solving' shuffles EVERSORUDE plus O (the top of 'Oxford's') and MAN. The whole clue also describes the character: the curmudgeonly chief inspector of Colin Dexter's Oxford novels and the TV series.
explanation.definitionFit: Colin Dexter's irascible Oxford detective chief inspector is known in full by his rarely used first name plus surname.

clue.text: Five in a Choppers Con? Probably not

definitions.text: Five in a Choppers Con? Probably not

indicators.note: the word in tells us the Roman five sits within the false-teeth word

parts.note: choppers is slang for teeth, especially false ones: dentures
V is the Roman numeral for five
Con is short for Conservative, a Tory

explanation.surface: A spoof Famous Five title, the gang foiling a helicopter swindle: hardly a real one.
explanation.walkthrough: The Famous Five are Enid Blyton's child adventurers, whose books are titled 'Five Go to...' and the like. 'Five in a Choppers Con' sounds like one, but 'Probably not' admits it is invented.
explanation.definitionFit: A Famous Five book is a tale of thrilling escapades, the genre of yarn named here, and the made-up title is offered as an example.

clue.text: Facetious policy-maker greeting Northern banker with what sounds like "Eh up"

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the pieces are read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: hallo is a greeting
a banker is a river (it has banks); the Tay is a river in northern Britain, in Scotland

indicators.note: the letter A said aloud is like the exclamation eh

parts.note: eh is an exclamation which, said aloud, is the name of the letter A

explanation.surface: A joker greets a northern bank clerk with the Yorkshire hello 'Eh up'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eh up' looks like the northern English greeting, but 'Eh' gives A by sound and 'up' reverses the whole run. 'Northern banker' is a Scottish river, not a teller.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers allows a loose, jocular sense of the Iranian religious title: any ideological leader or dogmatic policy-maker.

clue.text: To carry heavy load knight must stop for a breather

indicators.note: to stop something is to plug it, so the knight's letter goes in as a stopper

parts.note: to lug is to haul something heavy
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A knight lugging heavy armour has to pause for breath.
explanation.definitionFit: The organ of respiration is a breathing apparatus, so a breather in the literal sense.

clue.text: Old city crook shifting international violin cases

indicators.note: the violin word encases the other piece, holding it inside

parts.note: a Strad is a Stradivarius violin

indicators.note: shifting the international's letter means moving it out of the word for crook

parts.note: crook is informal for ill, poorly: ailing

explanation.surface: A conman in the old quarter swapping the cases of valuable foreign violins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crook' is not a criminal but the British and Australian informal word for unwell; 'shifting' removes the I from it before 'cases' wraps the violin round what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet name, from 1925 to 1961, of the city on the Volga now called Volgograd, scene of the great WWII battle.

clue.text: Perhaps reading all of the letters, this man would need help

parts.note: reading is one of the three Rs, so R stands for it, 'Perhaps' flagging the example

indicators.note: to need something is to be without it, so the help word is missing from the letters word

parts.note: every letter from A to Z is the alphabet
to abet is to help

explanation.surface: Someone who reads through every letter in a heap would need assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: The three Rs are reading, writing and arithmetic, so R can stand for reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A common boy's given name, so 'this man' is any fellow who bears it.

clue.text: Didn't you fancy engaging special nuclear defence outfit?

indicators.note: engaging means holding inside, so the shuffled letters take the special's letter in
fancy as an adjective means elaborate or fanciful, so these letters are given a fancy rearrangement

explanation.surface: A flirt asks whether you were attracted to someone special in protective gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' reads as the British verb for being attracted to someone, but it is the anagram signal for 'Didn't you'.
explanation.definitionFit: Military slang for the protective overgarment worn against nuclear, biological and chemical attack.

clue.text: Local papers going after a sucker

indicators.note: going after means the other pieces come after the a in the word

parts.note: a local is a pub, a public house: PH
papers, identity documents, give ID

explanation.surface: The local newspapers pursue a gullible person.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the local' is one's nearest pub, abbreviated PH on maps.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenfly and similar insects feed by piercing plants and drawing out sap, so they are sap-sucking pests.

clue.text: Detailed take on pinching Grand Hotel key

indicators.note: pinching means nicking or squeezing in, so the hiring word holds the two letters

parts.note: to take on staff is to hire them
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds
H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the key to a puzzle is its solution

explanation.surface: A careful view of a hotel thief pocketing a guest's room key.
explanation.definitionFit: An image or screen with fine resolution shows much detail, so it is highly detailed.

clue.text: They've new crude record, done with piercing cries

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record
over means finished, done

indicators.note: piercing means stabbing into, so the with letter goes into the cries word

parts.note: yells are loud cries

explanation.surface: A new and nasty album, finished with shrill screams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crude' looks like an adjective for the record, but it is crude oil, the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Exploratory boreholes that strike a new oil field are the first to tap fresh petroleum deposits.

clue.text: Consultant has no power to influence operation

indicators.note: has no means the consultant word lacks the power letter

parts.note: a consultant is an expert brought in to advise
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A consultant without authority can still sway a surgical procedure.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to bring a force or influence to bear, putting it into active operation.

clue.text: Fast runner does it to slow runner (since there's something very exciting about tortoises)

indicators.note: about means around, so the exciting thing goes around the other pieces

parts.note: a gas is informal for something great fun or thrilling

parts.words: Fast runner does it to slow runner
parts.note: a fast runner laps a slower one, going a whole circuit ahead
ago means since, back in time

explanation.surface: A hare overtaking a tortoise in a race, with a thrilling aside about tortoises.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the hare-and-tortoise fable. The definition is a language fact: the islands are named from the Spanish galápago, a tortoise, after the giant ones living there.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pacific archipelago takes its Spanish name from the giant land turtles found there, galápagos meaning tortoises.

clue.text: Five types stressing about missing mixed gin and tonic

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five

indicators.note: missing means the about letter is lost from the typeface word

parts.note: italics are the sloping typefaces used to stress words
C is short for circa, about

indicators.note: mixed means the drink's letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A pub-quiz scene: five people, hard on mixed gin and tonic, are stressed about missing out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gin and tonic' looks like one drink, but 'and' splits it: 'mixed gin' gives ING and 'tonic' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective a tonic is invigorating, something that restores energy and bodily vigour.

clue.text: Pen and record modern music with Hollies' principal writer

parts.note: a pen for pigs is a sty
a log is a written record
rap is a modern musical style

indicators.note: principal means first, so the leading letter of the band's name

explanation.surface: Stationery and recording by a 1960s pop group's lead songwriter.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hollies were a British 1960s pop group.
explanation.definitionFit: An old type of fountain pen with a tubular point instead of a nib, so an instrument for writing.

clue.text: Prow dismantled from freight ship

indicators.note: the prow is the front of a ship, so the front letter is knocked off the freight word

parts.note: freight is a cargo

explanation.surface: A cargo vessel has its bow taken apart.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Jason and the Argonauts sailed for the Golden Fleece in a vessel of this name.

clue.text: I'm hearing Joe Public's allowed to attend

definitions.text: I'm hearing Joe Public's allowed to attend

parts.words: I'm hearing Joe Public's allowed to attend
parts.note: a legal session the ordinary public may sit in on, speaking as if it were the court itself, which hears cases

explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm hearing' sounds like gossip being passed on, but the speaker is a court, which hears cases; 'Joe Public' is the ordinary citizen.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal session not held in camera: members of the general public may sit in and watch proceedings.

clue.text: At back of library, badly-educated set? No

parts.note: someone unread has read little, and so is poorly educated

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter, here placed after the other piece

explanation.surface: In the back of a library, a group of ill-educated people turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set' looks like a noun, a group of people, but it is the adjective, prepared; '? No' negates it.
explanation.definitionFit: Not prepared is the plain sense; it is also the epithet of the English king Æthelred.

clue.text: Fast counter service accepting orders for payment

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the service word holds the orders

parts.note: a rite is a religious service
POs are postal orders, used to send payments

explanation.surface: A fast-food counter service that takes payment by order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast counter' is not a quick shop counter but a quick comeback; postal orders are British money orders bought at a post office.
explanation.definitionFit: A swift retort, or in fencing a quick return thrust after parrying, so a counter delivered fast.

clue.text: New wine has an obligation to smell

definitions.meaning: freshly pressed grape juice before or during fermentation
the modal verb of necessity, as in 'she has to go'

explanation.surface: A young wine is obliged to have a bouquet.
explanation.definitionFit: Three senses: unfermented grape juice, the modal verb of obligation, and a word for mustiness or mould.

clue.text: Colony resettled with new land formation

indicators.note: a colony resettled is one moved and put down again, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Settlers move their colony to fresh territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with new land' reads as part of the anagram signal; 'new' simply suggests the rearrangement again.
explanation.definitionFit: A geological formation: the stiff Eocene clay bed underlying the English capital and the Thames basin.

clue.text: Do what my boss does with hot girl

parts.note: the setter's boss on a newspaper is the editor, who edits
H is the tap abbreviation for hot

explanation.surface: An employee copying the boss by chasing an attractive young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter speaks as a newspaper contributor, whose boss is the editor.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, so any girl bearing it fits.

clue.text: As is characteristic of art critics, each asked for more of the same

definitions.text: As is characteristic of art critics, each
definitions.meaning: a cryptic sense: the word characteristic is the letters of art critics plus each put into a fresh sequence, which is what the answer says happened

definitions.text: asked for more of the same
definitions.meaning: placed a repeat order for the identical thing

explanation.surface: Art critics, true to type, each demanded another helping.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a reverse-style cryptic hint: 'characteristic' is ART CRITICS and EACH shuffled, and the answer describes that. The second half is a plain definition: ordered again.
explanation.definitionFit: Placing a second order for an identical item is ordering it again, asking for more.

clue.text: To begin with, ducks have feathers

indicators.note: to begin with points to the first letter of the next word

parts.note: to own is to have

explanation.surface: Ducks start life with a covering of plumage.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft fine plumage, the fluffy under-feathers of birds such as eider ducks.

clue.text: Certainly not vanilla stout regular's drinking

indicators.note: drinking means swallowing, so the answer sits within the pub regular's words

explanation.surface: A pub regular drinking stout is anything but bland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vanilla' in slang means plain or conventional, so 'certainly not vanilla' is bizarre.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang vanilla means ordinary or bland; this borrowed French word means eccentric, far beyond the conventional.

clue.text: Torture screened by alien land

indicators.note: screened by means hidden behind, so the torture word sits inside the alien

parts.note: ET is the film's extra-terrestrial alien
gyp is British informal for pain, as in 'giving me gyp'

explanation.surface: An abduction story: an alien torturing a victim on its screens.
explanation.walkthrough: GYP is British slang for pain or torment.
explanation.definitionFit: A country in north-east Africa, a land of pyramids along the Nile.

clue.text: Might as well start off lifeboat drill?

parts.note: might means strength, power
too means as well

indicators.note: the start of the word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A lifeboat crew might as well begin their emergency practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drill' looks like an exercise, but it is the electric tool; the question mark flags that it is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: An electric drill is an example of a motor-driven hand tool.
